description: A shimmering new-wave love song from A Flock of Seagulls' 1982 debut album — guitarist Paul Reynolds named it because it simply sounded like a space-age love song, and it became a US Top 30 hit.

pops.text: Released on 28 May 1982, this was a single from the band's self-titled debut album. The Liverpool quartet was about to become one of MTV's defining early acts.
The band had written and recorded the song but couldn't title it. Guitarist Paul Reynolds suggested 'Space Age Love Song' because, he said, it sounded like a space age love song. It stuck.
All four members share the songwriting credit: Mike Score, his brother Ali Score, Frank Maudsley and Paul Reynolds. Mike Howlett produced the track.
Mike Score has described the song as being about intimacy — that instant eye contact across a crowded room when the chemistry is right. 'I saw your eyes and you made me smile' sums it up.
Score and Maudsley had both worked as hairdressers before the band took off. That styling background helps explain the most famous haircut in new wave, visible all over this video.
The 1982 video was directed by Tony van den Ende and shot at New York's Danceteria nightclub, with the band miming a performance on the club's rooftop.
Chart check: the song reached No. 30 on the US Billboard Hot 100 and No. 34 in the band's native UK. A slow-burner — its US peak came in February 1983.
It travelled well beyond the Anglo charts, too: No. 31 in New Zealand and No. 68 in Australia, where the band's singles consistently found an audience.
In 2018 the song was re-recorded with the Prague Philharmonic Orchestra as the first single from Ascension, the original lineup's first album together since 1984.
The 2018 reunion video was a reunion in fact, not just name: the album was made in separate studios worldwide, and Mike Score said filming was the first time all four had been together since 2004.

title: Space Age Love Song

description: A Flock of Seagulls' signature hit from their 1982 debut album — a UFO poster, a Liverpool club night and MTV's foil-covered video turned it into a US Top 10 and Australian No. 1 single.

pops.text: Released on 5 March 1982 as the band's third single, this opens their self-titled debut album. It remains their most successful single ever.
Mike Score cites two sparks. At Liverpool's Eric's Club, the band heard another group play a song called 'I Ran' — they loved the title, if not the song itself.

Spark two came the next day: a 1950s-style poster at the Zoo Records office showing a man and woman fleeing a flying saucer. The band wanted it for their album cover — and it fed the song's sci-fi lyrics.
The lyric follows a man transfixed by a woman, an aurora in the sky, and then a beam of light: yes, the love story ends in an alien abduction.
The long album version, at 5:07, opens with swirling synthesizer noises meant to imitate seagulls before the band kicks in. The video edit trims it to just under four minutes.

Director Tony van den Ende shot this video in a room lined with aluminium foil and mirrors. Look closely and you can spot the cameras reflected in the floor mirrors — budget sci-fi, perfectly on brand.
That haircut belonged to a trained professional: singer-keyboardist Mike Score and bassist Frank Maudsley were both former hairdressers.
America ran with it: No. 9 on the Billboard Hot 100, helped hugely by MTV. Rolling Stone's 'Second British Invasion' survey said the band 'struck gold on the first try.'
Australia ran furthest of all — the song topped the Australian chart, and reached No. 7 in New Zealand. At home in the UK, though, it stalled at No. 43.
The UK did eventually honour it with a silver certification from the BPI, despite that modest No. 43 peak. Germany, for the record, took it to No. 31.

title: I Ran (So Far Away)

description: Aerosmith's breakthrough Top 40 hit from Toys in the Attic (1975) — built on Tom Hamilton's years-old bass riff, a talk box, a bass marimba and a sugar packet shaken in place of maracas.

pops.text: Released as a single on 19 May 1975 from Toys in the Attic, this was written by Steven Tyler and bassist Tom Hamilton and produced by Jack Douglas at New York's Record Plant.
Hamilton first developed that famous bass riff in high school, after listening to Jeff Beck's 'Rice Pudding.' He then sat on it for years before the band ever heard it.
Tyler initially rejected it, telling Hamilton his early version was 'backward.' The riff only got its chance when Douglas declared a jam day near the end of the Toys sessions for any stray ideas.
That low, woody thump isn't bass alone: engineer Jay Messina doubled Hamilton's line on bass marimba, an instrument so deep its longest bars are played from a ladder, a full octave below the bass.
No maracas in the studio drum kit? No problem. Tyler shook a packet of sugar into a loud microphone instead — he is literally credited on the song for 'sugar packet.'
Tyler also plays the vibraslap in the intro — and broke it on the third hit. He later told Howard Stern you can hear it break in the finished recording.
Joe Perry's guitar 'sings' the title through a talk box unit called The Bag, made by Kustom Electronics. Tyler then joins in, singing the same line in unison with the guitar.
Some of Tyler's lyrics were aimed at tensions around Joe Perry's wife Elyssa — Tyler later clarified in the band autobiography Walk This Way that only some lines were inspired by her.
It became Aerosmith's first Top 40 single, peaking at No. 36 on the Billboard Hot 100. Its success prompted the band to re-release 'Dream On' — which then climbed to No. 6.
In 1991 David Thoener remixed the original recording for a re-release tied to the Pandora's Box set, with louder drums and a brand-new video. The remix later appeared on the Armageddon soundtrack.

title: Sweet Emotion

description: Steven Tyler's teenage piano sonnet became Aerosmith's signature power ballad — a No. 59 single in 1973 that, re-released three years later, climbed to No. 6 and launched the band.

pops.text: Written solely by Steven Tyler, this was a single from Aerosmith's self-titled 1973 debut album, first released on 27 June 1973. Tyler has called it a song about dreaming until your dreams come true.
Tyler began it at 17 or 18, roughly four years before Aerosmith existed, on a Steinway upright at Trow-Rico Lodge in Sunapee, New Hampshire, the resort his family ran.
He'd been playing too much in C, he recalled, so he moved to F — 'when you're a kid, F is the greatest.' The little sonnet that followed was never meant to be a real song.

The classical feel is inherited: Tyler's father Victor was a Juilliard-trained pianist, and as a three-year-old Steven would lie under the piano listening. 'That's where I got that Dream On chord-age,' he wrote.
He wrote the first verse in Sunapee and finished the second on a balcony at a hotel near Boston's Logan Airport, just before the band recorded it.
Aerosmith recorded it in October 1972 at Intermedia Studios in Boston, produced by Adrian Barber, for their January 1973 debut album.
First time around, the single stalled at No. 59 on the Billboard Hot 100 — though Boston radio played it heavily, keeping the song alive locally.
Re-released in late 1975, it finally peaked at No. 6 on 10 April 1976. The three-year-old ballad became Aerosmith's first major hit.
In 2018 the song was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame, 45 years after its release — recognition for a recording of lasting historical and cultural significance.

Eminem sampled its theme and Tyler's chorus for his 2002 hit 'Sing for the Moment,' with Joe Perry adding a new guitar solo. In 2022 Tyler joined Eminem to perform it live at Eminem's Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction.

title: Dream On

description: Denver funk outfit Analog Son's feel-good instrumental from Funky Mother (2018) — track three on the band's Color Red debut, named for guitarist Jordan Linit's desk-drawer French bulldog.

pops.text: This is track three on Funky Mother, released 28 September 2018. It follows the scene-setting instrumental 'CTI' and the vocal track 'Ugly Mug' in the album's upbeat opening run.

Denver band, old friendship: Analog Son was founded by guitarist Jordan Linit and bassist Josh Fairman, who started playing together at fourteen — their parents used to drop them off to play in local bars.
Before Analog Son, Linit and Fairman played together in Kinetix, a blend of rock, funk and pop. Analog Son was their chance to make funk the main event.
The title is a pet tribute: in a FunkCity interview, Linit explained it references a French bulldog he had that used to chill in his desk drawer while he wrote music.
Funky Mother was Analog Son's fourth album, but their first for Color Red — the label and platform founded by Eddie Roberts of The New Mastersounds.
Roberts also produced the album. Reviewers heard his fingerprints here, noting the guitar intro on 'Puppified' sounds like Roberts, or at least his influence.
The album was recorded and engineered at Scanhope Sound in the Denver area — a studio owned by the band's own bassist and co-leader, Josh Fairman.
And it was cut the old-school way: Linit told FunkCity the record was recorded together as a live session, band in the room rather than part by part.

By this album the band's rotating cast had solidified: Devon Parker and Ashley Niven on vocals, Eric Luba on keyboards, George Horn on drums, Will Trask on percussion, Mike Chiesa on tenor sax and Gabe Mervine on trumpet.

Critics singled out this track's horn-to-guitar groove, Linit's guitar bridge in the middle, and its build to a hard-stop ending. The album launched with a release party at Denver's Cervantes' Masterpiece Ballroom on 28 September 2018.

title: Puppified

description: A five-minute funk workout from Analog Son's second album Stomp and Shout — track two, all horns, keys and groove from Denver's rotating-cast funk supergroup.

pops.text: Welcome to the Gun Show — no firearms, just flexing. This is track two of Stomp and Shout, Analog Son's second album, released March 7, 2015.
Analog Son is the brainchild of guitarist Jordan Linit and bassist Josh Fairman, both from Kinetix. Live for Live Music calls the project a Colorado funk supergroup.
Linit and Fairman have played together since they were 12 years old. They came to Denver to study music in their teens — and basically never left the groove.
This is a rotating-cast band by design: Linit and Fairman wrote the tunes intending each album and performance to feature a new lineup and a fresh improvisational approach.
The Stomp and Shout cast is stacked: Ryan Zoidis and Eric Bloom — the Shady Horns from Lettuce — plus Nigel Hall, Joe Tatton of the New Mastersounds and Ivan Neville.
Reviewers singled this track out: Live for Live Music said 'Gun Show' is where the album really finds its legs, a five-minute roller coaster with the keyboards taking the reins in the solo.
No one instrument hogs the spotlight here. That same review notes every instrument is vital, even if the horns mostly determine the melody.
The name fits the method: Fairman co-founded Scanhope Sound in Colorado, built by combining new recording technology with the analog gear their favorite records were made on.
How funky did this album get? Its title track brought in four keyboardists at once. 'Gun Show' is cut from that same maximal cloth.
The album launched live on release night, March 7, 2015, at Denver's Bluebird Theater, with Nigel Hall and Jason Hann of the String Cheese Incident joining the show.

title: Gun Show

description: A heavy, socially conscious deep cut from Travelers and Thieves, Blues Traveler's second album — track three, written by Chan Kinchla and John Popper, and never a single.

pops.text: Deep-cut alert: 'Ivory Tusk' is track three of Travelers and Thieves, Blues Traveler's second album, released September 3, 1991 on A&M Records.
Chan Kinchla and John Popper wrote it, and it runs 5:15 — a full, jam-ready album track, not a radio edit. It was never released as a single.
The album's singles were 'All in the Groove,' 'Sweet Pain' and 'Mountain Cry.' 'Ivory Tusk' stayed an album listener's discovery.
Trouser Press called 'Onslaught' and 'Ivory Tusk' heavy — in tone and in their socially conscious lyrics — a sterner sound than the band's good-natured grooves.
Listen to the low end: a later deep-dive on the album praised Bobby Sheehan's bass on this track as flowing, almost fretless, and melodic rather than simple roots-rock thump.
The album was produced by Jim Gaines with the band, and runs a generous 61 minutes and 25 seconds across 12 tracks.
Session credits are pure Popper: besides vocals and harmonica, he's credited with 12-string acoustic guitar, calymba, and — officially — various barks, squeaks, growls and whistles.
Odd catalog quirk: on iTunes the album is listed only as Travelers, because the full title is split across two drawings — one on the cover, one inside the liner notes.
The liner notes include a poem, 'Of Travelers & Thieves,' written by Jonathan Sheehan — brother of bassist Bobby Sheehan.
It held up live: a November 21, 1997 review from Chicago's Aragon Ballroom has Blues Traveler pounding through 'Ivory Tusk' to open their first set.

title: Ivory Tusk

description: Blues Traveler's first single and the lead track of their 1990 debut — written by teenagers in high school, then a surprise Top 40 hit six years later via Kingpin.

pops.text: This was written by accident in high school. Chan Kinchla later explained the verse riff began as him just checking how his amp sounded — and the band said, 'That sounds cool, what's that?'
They were 17 years old. Kinchla played the riff again, changed the chords a little, and John Popper wrote lyrics immediately, sitting right there. They played it that way ever since.
It's the lead track and first single from the band's self-titled debut, released in May 1990 and recorded in February–March 1990. Writers: Kinchla and Popper.
First time around, its home was college radio: the debut got 'But Anyway' airplay on college stations while the band built its name on the road.
The debut album had a future star in the background: Joan Osborne sang backing vocals on two of its tracks.
Six years later, Hollywood called. Blues Traveler performed 'But Anyway' over the closing credits of the 1996 comedy Kingpin — dressed in traditional Amish clothing.
The official video stitches it together: live footage of the band at different venues, close-ups, and short clips from Kingpin.
Second life, real charts: in summer 1996 it peaked at No. 5 on Billboard's Adult Alternative Airplay chart and No. 24 on Mainstream Top 40.
Grammar nerds, rejoice: the song is basically an adverb with a band behind it, repeating 'but anyway' through the lyric as Popper shrugs his way forward.
In 2007 the band revisited it for Cover Yourself, their fan-poll hits album in new acoustic arrangements — and tried making it more of a rock song before finding the groove changed the melody.

title: But Anyway

description: The opening track of Infidels, Dylan's 1983 return to secular music — a reggae-tinged, Bible-haunted riddle recorded with Mark Knopfler, Mick Taylor and Sly & Robbie.

pops.text: 'Jokerman' opens Infidels, released October 27, 1983 — Dylan's first secular album after his three evangelical, born-again records.
Dylan told Rolling Stone's Kurt Loder it came to him in the Caribbean: 'Me and another guy have a boat down there… It's very mystical,' inspired by spirits called jumbis.
It was recorded April 14, 1983 at the Power Station in New York, produced by Dylan with Dire Straits' Mark Knopfler — who also plays guitar.
That's an all-star band: ex-Rolling Stone Mick Taylor on guitar, Alan Clark on keyboards, and reggae's great rhythm section, Robbie Shakespeare on bass and Sly Dunbar on drums.
Knopfler got the job after Dylan had spoken with David Bowie, Frank Zappa and Elvis Costello about producing the album.
Who is the Jokerman? Critics have read him as a false messiah, a political manipulator of crowds, and a sly self-portrait — the song's biblical imagery supports almost endless interpretations.
The video, released March 27, 1984, was directed by ad legend George Lois and produced by Larry 'Ratso' Sloman. Dylan lip-syncs only the choruses.
The verses play as an art-history slideshow: photos of Hitler, Ronald Reagan and Muhammad Ali, plus paintings by Hieronymus Bosch, Francisco Goya and Albrecht Dürer.
On March 22, 1984, Dylan tore through 'Jokerman' on Late Night with David Letterman, backed by members of L.A. punk band the Plugz — harmonica-in-the-wrong-key scramble included.
Letterman loved that performance so much he asked if they could come back every Thursday. A decade later, 'Jokerman' was opening Dylan's set at Woodstock '94.

title: Jokerman

description: Dylan's dreamy 1965 original from Bringing It All Back Home — written after Mardi Gras, inspired by a wagon-wheel tambourine, and soon eclipsed by the Byrds' No. 1 cover.

pops.text: The tambourine man was real: guitarist Bruce Langhorne. Dylan said Langhorne had 'this gigantic tambourine… as big as a wagon wheel,' and the image stuck in his mind.
Dylan began the song in February 1964 after attending Mardi Gras in New Orleans on a cross-country road trip, and finished it by late April.
He debuted it live in London, at the Royal Festival Hall on May 17, 1964 — nearly a year before it appeared on an album.
He first recorded it in June 1964 for Another Side of Bob Dylan, with Ramblin' Jack Elliott, but held it back. That early version surfaced decades later on a Bootleg Series release.
The released take was recorded January 15, 1965. The only accompaniment is Langhorne himself, playing the gentle electric guitar countermelody.
It's the first track of the acoustic side of Bringing It All Back Home, released March 22, 1965. Dylan never released his own version as a single.
The Byrds recorded their cover just five days after Dylan's final version, on January 20, 1965 — after hearing his publisher's demo with Ramblin' Jack Elliott.
Roger McGuinn rebuilt it for radio: a rock beat, his jangly 12-string Rickenbacker, and just one of Dylan's four verses. Dylan heard it in rehearsal and reportedly said you could dance to it.
Only one Byrd played an instrument on their hit: McGuinn. Session pros the Wrecking Crew — including Hal Blaine and Leon Russell — played the rest, with Crosby and Clark on harmonies.
The Byrds' single, released April 12, 1965, hit No. 1 on both the Billboard Hot 100 and the UK chart and helped invent folk rock — a hit Dylan himself never had with the song.

title: Mr. Tambourine Man

description: Seger's wistful look back at a dancer he watched through a club window as a kid in Ann Arbor. Cut in Muscle Shoals for the breakthrough Night Moves, it became a classic-rock radio staple.

pops.text: Plot twist in the title: Seger has said the street is really Ann Street, just off Main Street in Ann Arbor, Michigan, where he grew up.
Seger recalled a pool hall on that corner where girls danced in the window and R&B bands played on weekends — a whole world to a kid stuck outside.
One act he watched through the glass stuck with him: Washboard Willie, a Chicago-style blues outfit that played the club regularly.
Seger called the song his 'awakening' — after being a quiet, awkward kid, this corner was where the grown-up world first came into focus.
Surprise: the Silver Bullet Band isn't the band on this record. Seger cut 'Mainstreet' at Muscle Shoals Sound Studio in Sheffield, Alabama.
The players were the Muscle Shoals Rhythm Section — Barry Beckett on keyboards, David Hood on bass, Roger Hawkins on drums and Jimmy Johnson on rhythm guitar.
That lonely, echoing guitar intro is Pete Carr, the Muscle Shoals session guitarist who also played on Paul Simon's 'Kodachrome.'
Hear it live and the intro changes: in concert, Carr's famous guitar opening was replaced with a saxophone intro.
Released in April 1977 as a single from Night Moves, following the title track — two straight singles built on looking backward.
It peaked at No. 24 on the Billboard Hot 100 but went all the way to No. 1 in Canada. Parent album Night Moves peaked at No. 8 and made Seger a superstar.

title: Mainstreet

description: A Midwestern kid gets dazzled and dropped by Los Angeles in the breathless opener to Stranger in Town. Double drums, gospel-tinged backing vocals, and a chorus that arrived while Seger was driving.

pops.text: This is the opening track of Stranger in Town (1978) — it kicks the album off at full speed and never really slows down.
The chorus arrived while Seger was driving in the Hollywood Hills. He turned the car around, drove home repeating 'Don't forget it — don't turn on the radio!' and sang it into a cassette recorder.
Back at his rented house sat a Time magazine dated March 6, 1978, with model Cheryl Tiegs on the cover, billed as 'The All-American Model.'
Tiegs became the template: Seger decided to write about a guy from the Midwest who meets someone like her and gets caught up in the whole 'bizarro thing.'
The romance in the song is invented — a whirlwind that ends with the hero waking up alone, looking over the hills and wondering if he can ever go home.
It was recorded in 1977 at Cherokee Studios in Hollywood — fitting for a song Seger wrote while finishing the album in Los Angeles.
That relentless beat is one drummer, twice: David Teegarden recorded a full drum pass, then overdubbed a different pattern on top, so it sounds like two drummers at once.
Little Feat keyboardist Bill Payne played piano and organ on the track, giving the rocker a rolling, churchy push.
The backing vocals are the Waters family — Julia, Luther, Maxine and Oren Waters, session royalty who also backed Lionel Richie, Bruce Springsteen and Barbra Streisand.
Issued in July 1978 as the album's second single, with 'Brave Strangers' on the B-side, it peaked at No. 12 in the US and No. 42 in the UK. Stranger in Town itself hit No. 4.

title: Hollywood Nights

description: The quietest, spookiest song on Born in the U.S.A. — a barely-two-and-a-half-minute whisper of desire built on a Johnny Cash rhythm, an on-the-spot arrangement, and one very loaded Thunderbird.

pops.text: This was recorded in 1982, during the first wave of Born in the U.S.A. sessions at The Power Station in New York — two years before the album came out.
Some of its lyrics had an earlier life: Springsteen had written them for an unreleased song called 'Spanish Eyes,' dating back to the Darkness on the Edge of Town era.
The groove is a tribute: Springsteen started playing a slow, Johnny Cash-inspired rhythm on guitar and the song fell out around it.
Drummer Max Weinberg and pianist Roy Bittan were hearing it for the first time — they built their accompaniment on the spot, and that take's feel stuck.
The result mixes a soft rockabilly beat with synthesizers — one of the first uses of synths in Springsteen's music, and it gives the song its hazy, late-night glow.
On the album it closes side one of Born in the U.S.A. — the quiet smolder right after all that side's stadium-sized shouting.
Released as a single on February 6, 1985, its B-side was 'Johnny Bye Bye,' Springsteen's adaptation of Chuck Berry's 'Bye Bye Johnny.'
It peaked at No. 6 on the Billboard Hot 100 — the fourth of a record-tying seven Top 10 singles pulled from Born in the U.S.A.
In the Netherlands it spent three weeks at No. 1 in August 1985, while two other Springsteen singles sat in the Dutch Top 10 at the same time.
Johnny Cash eventually closed the circle: the man whose rhythm inspired the song covered it in 2000 for the tribute album Badlands: A Tribute to Bruce Springsteen's Nebraska.

title: I'm On Fire

description: Springsteen's first Top 10 hit was almost a Ramones song. A one-night write, a sped-up vocal and the Turtles' duo on backing vocals turned it into the pop breakthrough of The River.

pops.text: This was written for somebody else: after seeing the Ramones in Asbury Park, Joey Ramone asked Springsteen to write them a song — and he went home and wrote this that night.
Then it nearly left anyway. In his Greatest Hits liner notes Springsteen wrote that he played it for manager Jon Landau, who, 'earning his money,' advised him to keep it.
The title is borrowed finery: it comes from a line in Tennyson's poem 'Ulysses' — 'For always roaming with a hungry heart.'
Listen closely to the voice: Springsteen's vocal was slightly sped up on the recording, nudging it higher and poppier than his natural register.
Those sighing backing vocals belong to Flo & Eddie — Mark Volman and Howard Kaylan of the Turtles, who'd hit No. 1 themselves with 'Happy Together.'
The golden glow is E Street machinery: Danny Federici's organ up front, Roy Bittan's piano, and Clarence Clemons adding saxophone.
It was the first single from The River, Springsteen's double album — which went on to become his first No. 1 album on the Billboard chart.
It peaked at No. 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1980 — Springsteen's first-ever Top 10 hit, five years after Born to Run made him famous without a hit single.
The B-side, 'Held Up Without A Gun,' didn't appear on The River — it started Springsteen's tradition of using non-album songs as B-sides.

Live, the crowd does the work: Springsteen lets the audience sing the first verse and chorus before he joins in, a ritual that grew out of River Tour shows. The song also turned up in Tom Cruise's Risky Business (1983).

title: Hungry Heart

description: Winston Rodney takes on greed and overdevelopment — in Jamaica and far beyond — on this deep cut from Appointment With His Majesty, the Grammy-nominated 1997 album from reggae's elder statesman.

pops.text: This is track 10 on Appointment With His Majesty (1997), and it runs a patient 5:21 — roots reggae in no hurry to make its point.
Every song on the album was written and arranged by Winston Rodney himself — as ever, Burning Spear is a one-man ministry of message music.
Stereo Review singled this track out, saying 'Commercial Development' and 'Don't Sell Out' 'strike back at the industrialization of both Jamaica and reggae.'
The target isn't only Jamaica: the Houston Press noted the song is as much about Houston as Jamaica, singing of greed and corruption undermining the social fabric.
The album earned a Grammy nomination for Best Reggae Album at the 40th Grammy Awards in 1998 — one of many nominations before Rodney finally won.
It also charted: Appointment With His Majesty peaked at No. 10 on Billboard's Reggae Albums chart.
Critics heard the mission plainly — The Washington Post called the album 'first and foremost message music,' over what the Boston Globe described as mesmerizing bass lines and snappy horns.
Rodney comes from Saint Ann's Bay, Jamaica — the same parish that produced both Bob Marley and Marcus Garvey, the twin poles of his music.
His career started with a tip: in 1969, fellow Saint Ann native Bob Marley advised Rodney to approach Coxsone Dodd's Studio One label, which released his debut single, 'Door Peep.'
The nominations eventually paid off: Burning Spear went on to win Grammy Awards for Calling Rastafari and Jah Is Real, confirming the elder-statesman status this album already shows.

title: Commercial Development
